Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe injuries associated with a knee dislocation and review the evaluation of ligament and
neurovascular injuries.
Identify indications for acute open reduction or wound management.
Recognize injuries that require early management.
Review treatment options for acute, staged, or delayed repair/reconstruction.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Knee dislocations are a rare orthopedic injury; however, the incidence is likely
underrepresented in the literature. Several aspects of workup and initial management are

critical, but treatment strategies remain controversial.
Epidemiology
Knee dislocations represent less than 0.2% of all orthopaedic injuries.
The incidence reported in the literature likely is under-representative of the true incidence
because 20% to 50% of knee dislocations spontaneously reduce in the field.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology

Osteology
The distal femur is the main weight bearing surface along with the proximal tibia. On the
medial side, the convex femoral condyle is relatively congruent with the concave plateau.
On the lateral side, the concave femoral condyle articulates with a convex lateral
plateau. Therefore, knee stability is highly dependent on the surrounding soft tissues,
including the menisci and ligaments. The patella articulates anteriorly within the
trochlear groove of the distal femur. The proximal fibula and tibia also have a small
diarthrodial joint.
Vascular Anatomy
The relatively high incidence of neurovascular compromise in patients with a knee dislocation
is explained by the anatomy of the knee (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Illustration shows the posterior anatomy of the knee. Note the relationship between the
popliteal artery and the tibial and common peroneal nerves. (Reproduced from Good L, Johnson
RJ: The dislocated knee. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1995;3[5]:284-292.)

Vascular Anatomy
The femoral artery travels through the adductor hiatus, where it is relatively immobile,
and then becomes the popliteal artery in the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee.
Distally, the popliteal artery is tethered at the fibrous arch deep to the soleus muscle.
Nerves
The common peroneal nerve travels along the posterior edge of the biceps femoris and
continues distally around the fibular neck. The tibial nerve, after branching from the sciatic
nerve, courses distally through the center of the popliteal fossa.
The tibial nerve runs within the popliteal fossa along with the popliteal artery

Tendons
Tendons
Tendons that cross the knee joint allow motion and provide secondary stability. The patellar
tendon extends from the distal patella to the tibia tubercle. Medially, the pes anserinus
(sartorius, gracilis and semi-tendinosis) and the semimembranosus insert on the proximal tibia.
Laterally, the bicep femoris inserts on the posterolateral fibula, and the popliteus attaches to the
lateral femur. Posteriorly, the gastrocnemius tendons insert into the distal femur. Any of these
tendonous structures can be avulsed during a high-energy knee dislocation and require
reattachment to support knee joint stability and motion.
Joints and Ligaments
The stability of the knee joint is provided by bony articulations and dynamic and static soft-
tissue stabilizers (Table 1).
The four major ligamentous stabilizers of the knee are the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL),
posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), medial collateral ligament (MCL), and fibular collateral
ligament (FCL).
Table 1 Soft-Tissue Stabilizers of the Knee
Structure
Function
ACL
Primary: resists anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur
Secondary: resists varus/valgus stresses in full extension
PCL
Primary: resists posterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur
Secondary: resists tibial external rotation
MCL
Resists valgus stress
PMC
Resists valgus stress
FCL
Resists varus stress
PLC
Resists posterior translation, external rotation, and varus angulation of the
tibia


Joints and Ligaments
The posterolateral corner (PLC), posteromedial corner (PMC), and the medial and lateral
menisci confer additional stability to the knee. The PLC consists of the FCL, iliotibial
band, popliteofibular ligament, biceps femoris, and popliteal tendon. The PMC consists
of the posterior oblique ligament, semimembranosus tendon, oblique popliteal
ligament, posteromedial joint capsule, and posterior horn of the medial meniscus
(Figures 2 and 3).

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
High-energy injuries include those from motor vehicle collisions, falls from a height, and
industrial accidents.
Low-energy injuries include sports-related injuries, often with a rotatory component.
Ultra-low–energy injuries include those occurring from seemingly trivial trauma in patients
with morbid obesity.
Risk Factors

Risk Factors
Surgeons should maintain a heightened awareness for a knee dislocation associated
with motorcycle accidents, all-terrain vehicle accidents, and a pedestrian struck by a car.
Approximately 5% to 15% of patients with ipsilateral acetabular, femoral, and tibial
fractures also have a ligamentous knee injury. Schatzker type IV medial shear fractures,
unicondylar femur fractures, periarticular tibial rim fractures, or PCL avulsions are
radiographic signs that should alert the clinician to consider additional knee ligament
damage (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Images show examples of injuries that suggest additional knee ligament
damage. A, AP knee radiograph demonstrates a Schatzker type IV medial shear fracture.
AP (B) and lateral (C) knee radiographs demonstrate a unicondylar femur fracture. D,

Associated Injuries
Vascular injury
Popliteal artery
Incidence in the literature ranges from 23% to 32%.
Signs of vascular injury (asymmetric pulses after reduction, active bleeding, expanding
hematoma, ankle-brachial index [ABI] <0.9) warrant immediate vascular surgery consultation
(Figure 5).
The ABI is systolic pressure measured at the ankle divided by systolic pressure measured at
the arm. To perform this test, a manual blood pressure cuff is used to obtain systolic blood
pressure at the arm. The same blood pressure cuff is used to measure systolic pressure on
the affected extremity at the ankle. Doppler should be used to assess the pulse. The ankle
systolic pressure is then divided by the arm systolic pressure. A normal ABI is greater than
0.9.

The Moore classification is used to describe tibial plateau fractures associated with knee
dislocations (Figure 11).
Type I: coronal split fracture
Type II: entire condyle fracture
Type III: rim avulsion fracture of the lateral plateau
Type IV: rim compression fracture
Type V: four-part fracture
Figure 11 Illustrations show the Moore classification of tibial plateau fractures. A, Split fracture of
the medial plateau in the coronal plane. B, Fracture of the entire condyle. C, Rim avulsion
fracture. D, Pure compression fracture. E, Four-part fracture. (Reproduced from Egol KA: Tibial

Extensor mechanism disruption
Reported in as many as 8.6% of patients


Associated Injuries
Initial physical examination may be normal in patients with an intimal flap tear; however,
such tears can propagate, resulting in complete arterial occlusion. All patients with
concern for a knee dislocation should undergo ABI measurements in the emergency
room. Angiography is unnecessary in patients with a normal physical examination and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Knee Dislocations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000536
13/43

ABI (≥0.9). The main indication for angiography is clinical signs of vascular injury without
limb-threatening ischemia. Patients with ischemia should be taken directly to the
operating room for evaluation by a vascular surgeon. Warm limb ischemia durations
longer than 6 hours are associated with a risk of amputation, and any revascularization
warrants prophylactic fasciotomies.
Common peroneal nerve injury most commonly occurs in patients with a posterolateral
dislocation. If the peroneal nerve recovers, improvement usually begins by 3 months
postinjury and is accompanied by a positive Tinel sign. Incomplete injuries and early
return of any function are associated with a good prognosis for nerve recovery.
Observation is the preferred treatment option for the management of incomplete
peroneal nerve palsies. If electromyographic testing is performed, a baseline study can
be obtained approximately 4 to 6 weeks postinjury; repeat electromyographic testing
can be performed at 3 months postinjury. Tibialis posterior transfer can be performed as
a salvage procedure to restore active dorsiflexion.
Chondral and meniscal injuries are common and should be evaluated via MRI and
managed during surgical treatment, if indicated.
Prevents immediate arthroscopic reconstruction because of fluid extravasation
concerns. May result in severe swelling of the calf.
Injury Classification
Frank knee dislocations are primarily described by the direction of the tibia dislocation, namely
anterior, posterior, medial, lateral, or rotatory (Figure 12). Rotatory dislocations can be further
subdivided into anteromedial, anterolateral, posteromedial, or posterolateral (Figure 13).

Figure 12 Lateral knee radiographs demonstrate anterior (A), posterior (B), and lateral (C) frank

Figure 13 Images show rotatory dislocations. A, AP knee radiograph demonstrates an
anteromedial rotatory dislocation. Clinical photograph (B) and AP (C) and lateral (D) radiographs
of a knee show an anterolateral rotatory dislocation. (Courtesy of William T. Obremskey, MD,
MPH, Nashville, TN.)

Injury Classification
Anterior dislocations are most common and result from a hyperextension mechanism of
injury, typically leading to a sequential rupture of the posterior capsule, PCL, and ACL.
Traction injury to the popliteal vessel leads to intimal damage. Posterior dislocations are
the second most common and result from a posteriorly directed force applied to the
proximal tibia, such as a dashboard injury. The popliteal artery may be transected by the
tibia. In rotatory dislocations, the PCL typically remains intact and serves as the rotary

This classification system defines the extent of ligamentous injury and considers

Clinical evaluation
In patients who sustain a high-energy mechanism of injury, other life-threatening injuries
may be present. Evaluation should follow Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol.
Clinicians should maintain a high clinical suspicion.
A thorough neurovascular examination should be performed.
After reduction, ligaments should be assessed (Resource 1).
ACL: positive Lachman test (Videos 1 and 2)
PCL: positive posterior drawer test (Video 3)
MCL: valgus laxity at 30° of knee flexion (Video 4)
PMC: positive posteromedial drawer test
FCL: varus laxity at 30° of knee flexion (Video 5)
PLC: positive posterolateral drawer test
Differentiating PLC injuries from combined PLC/PCL injuries: positive dial test (increased tibial
external rotation at 30° of flexion indicates PLC injury; increased tibial external rotation at 30°
and 90° of flexion indicates combined PLC/PCL injury)
Collateral ligament, one or more cruciate ligaments, and capsular injury: varus/valgus laxity at
full knee extension
PCL, PMC, PLC, and posterior capsule: positive supine heel-lift test

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Knee dislocation should be suspected in patients with uncontained hemarthrosis about
the knee, contusions, and gross laxity. In addition, any patient with two or more
ligamentous injuries or with certain fractures (PCL avulsion, proximal tibia rim avulsions,
Schatzker type IV) about the knee should be evaluated for a suspected knee dislocation.
A thorough neurovascular examination is essential. Pulses are assessed for symmetry
and, if symmetric, should be accompanied by the ABI. If these tests are normal (ABI
≥0.9), serial and frequent neurovascular examinations should be performed.
Neurovascular examination should be performed before and after reduction. If a
patient’s ABI is less than 0.9, then a CT angiography or angiography are indicated.
Ligamentous examination should proceed in a systematic fashion to identify disrupted
and intact structures. Table 3 lists the soft-tissue stabilizers of the knee, their function,
and the corresponding clinical tests for stability. The soft-tissue stabilizers of the knee
and the most sensitive clinical examination maneuvers that indicate disruption are listed
below.

Test

Patient History
The patient history will vary depending on the mechanism of injury; however, clinicians should
maintain a high level of suspicion for knee dislocation in patients describing subluxation
events.

9/3/26, 4:31 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000536
21/43

Clinicians also should be aware of ultra-low–velocity knee dislocations. These occur in patients
with morbid obesity who sustain a very low-energy mechanism of injury, including stepping off
a curb. High clinical suspicion often is necessary to detect these types of injuries, and diagnosis
may be delayed.
Physical Examination
Physical examination is a critical component of the workup in patients in whom a knee
dislocation is suspected. In patients with a frank dislocation, a neurovascular examination
should be obtained before prompt reduction. After reduction, a second neurovascular
examination should be performed. A comprehensive ligamentous examination should be
performed after the knee is reduced, including testing of the ACL, PCL, FCL, MCL, PLC, PMC,
and extensor mechanism. If the physical examination indicates a knee dislocation, then MRI
should be performed after vascular sufficiency is ensured.
Neurovascular Examination
Serial neurovascular examinations are a critical component of the acute workup for patients
with a knee dislocation.
The neurovascular examination should include an assessment of distal pulses compared with
those of the uninjured extremity. Any discrepancy should lead to a vascular consultation and
additional workup. ABI measurements should be obtained in patients with normal pulses. The
ABI is determined by manually measuring systolic blood pressure in the arm and the affected
leg. If the ratio of leg systolic blood pressure over arm systolic blood pressure is lower than
0.9, then additional workup is necessary. An ABI of less than 0.9 is 100% specific and sensitive
in predicting vascular injury in patients with a knee dislocation (Resource 2).
A thorough neurologic examination should also be performed, with particular attention paid to
peroneal nerve function.
Serial examinations should be performed within 24 hours postinjury to monitor for evolving
problems, such as compartment syndrome and subsequent vascular thrombus and
dysvascularity.
Imaging Studies
Radiography

AP and lateral radiographs should be obtained in all patients in whom a knee dislocation is
suspected. If this can be accomplished without substantial delay, radiographs should be
obtained before and after reduction attempts.
Stress radiographs obtained in the acute, chronic, and postoperative phases may provide
useful information with regard to treatment decisions. Stress radiographs are obtained using
fluoroscopy or standard radiography (Figure 14). The examiner applies varus, valgus, anterior,
or posterior force to the knee, and radiographs are obtained. This will provide a measure of
instability in various planes.
Figure 14 AP fluoroscopic images of a knee with stress applied show varus instability (A) and
lateral collateral ligament incompetence (B). (Courtesy of William T. Obremskey, MD, MPH,
Nashville, TN.)
Computed Tomography
May be useful in the acute setting for evaluation of associated fractures or in patients in whom
MRI is contraindicated (Figure 15)

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is used to evaluate ligamentous, capsular, meniscal, cartilaginous, and other soft-tissue
lesions, helping guide surgical management. MRI should be obtained as soon as logistically
and safely possible (Figure 16).

collateral ligament avulsion. B, Sagittal MRI shows a posterior cruciate ligament rupture. C,
Coronal MRI shows a medial collateral ligament avulsion. (Courtesy of William T. Obremskey, MD,
MPH, Nashville, TN.)
Other Imaging Studies

Some studies have suggested magnetic resonance angiography as an alternative to traditional
angiography in the acute setting.1 Similarly, CT angiography has been adopted by many
centers for use in the acute evaluation of knee dislocations because of its speed and accuracy.
Any patients with clear indications of vascular injury should be taken directly to the operating
room for treatment; CT angiography or magnetic resonance angiography may lead to an
unnecessary delay in management and can be performed more electively.
Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis for knee dislocations includes isolated ligamentous injury, distal
femur and tibial plateau fractures, and extensor mechanism disruption.
Management
Closed reduction

Management
Closed reduction is performed after neurovascular assessment and evaluation of plain
radiographs (Figure 17). The reduction maneuver involves axial limb traction with
translation of the tibia in the appropriate direction. For posterolateral dislocations in
which the medial femoral condyle has buttonholed or perforated through the medial
capsular structures (the dimple sign), closed reduction attempt should be avoided, and
the patient should be taken to the operating room for emergent open reduction (Figures
18 and 19).
After reduction, a knee immobilizer or splint is placed. Post-reduction radiographs
should be obtained. If reduction cannot be maintained in a splint or vascular repair is
required, then an external fixator is indicated.

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical treatment is indicated in patients unable to tolerate a surgical procedure and in
less active patients with a stable joint in a splint or brace.
Indications
Patients with morbid obesity who have joint stability on reduction.
Severe closed head injury or severe comorbidities that make surgical management too risky
(chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, aortic stenosis).

Contraindications
Gross knee instability on physical examination, persistent knee subluxation, open wounds,
associated periarticular fractures (patella, proximal tibia, distal femur).
Techniques/Procedures
Cast or brace with limited–weight bearing
Outcomes
A 2001 meta-analysis performed by Dedmond et al2 compared 132 knee dislocations managed
surgically with 74 knee dislocations managed nonsurgically. The authors reported improved
outcomes in the surgically managed group and recommended surgical treatment for patients
with a knee dislocation.
Surgical Management
Surgical treatment has been proven to lead to better patient-reported outcomes.
Management of associated PLC and PMC injuries is imperative to achieve good long-term
results with ACL/PCL reconstruction.
Several studies have reported good patient-reported outcome measures at follow-up of more
than 2 years;3 however, evidence of radiographic osteoarthritis has been reported to be as
high as 42% to 87% in some series at the same duration of follow-up.
Indications
Surgical treatment is indicated in the acute setting in physically active patients without medical
comorbidities that prohibit surgery. In the chronic setting, surgical treatment is indicated for
patients with knee instability who do not have substantial arthrosis.
Techniques/Procedures
Surgical treatment options include repair versus reconstruction, with repair reserved for acute
avulsions of the collateral ligaments. Some studies have begun to advocate for the repair of
cruciate avulsion injuries in select patient populations.1,4
Timing and materials for ligament reconstruction vary based on surgeon preference.

Knee Spanning External Fixator
Preoperative Planning
Knee spanning external fixators should be placed in any patient with a knee dislocation and
associated vascular injury requiring repair and any patient with a dislocation not appropriately
reduced in a knee immobilizer or plaster splint.

Preoperative Planning
The timing of external fixator placement should be discussed with the vascular team
before vascular repair. Occasionally, because of ipsilateral femur or tibia fractures, limb
stability will facilitate repair and will ensure that the leg is out to length and in
appropriate alignment. Some vascular surgeons prefer to approach a popliteal artery
injury posteriorly, particularly in patients with obesity, with the patient in the prone
position. An anterior external fixator is not feasible. The attending orthopaedic and
vascular surgeons should discuss the timing of repair and stabilization before surgical
management (Figure 20).

Bone foam, sheets, or a bump may be used to hold the leg in 20° to 30° of flexion.
Surgical Approaches

Surgical Approaches
Various acceptable knee spanning constructs can be used. The main goals should be to
attain appropriate length and alignment of the lower extremity and achieve concentric
knee reduction on fluoroscopic imaging. The location of the external fixator should be
discussed with the vascular team if placed before repair to ensure placement does not
impede access. Care should be taken to not place clamps directly in line with the joint
because it may lead to difficulty with future imaging studies.
Acute Repair
Preoperative Planning
Advanced imaging studies, including MRI, should be obtained to determine damaged
structures. The course of the peroneal nerve also can be assessed to protect it during
exposure.
Repairable structures should be determined. Avulsions and midsubstance ruptures of the
collateral ligaments may be acutely repaired. Midsubstance tears of the cruciate ligaments
may be better managed via reconstruction.
Patellar tendon tears, root avulsions, extruded menisci, flipped MCL, and fractures are difficult
to manage late (>3 weeks postinjury), and early surgical management is favored.
Patient Positioning
Supine on a radiolucent table
Surgical Approaches
Midline anterior incision with a medial parapatellar arthrotomy
An accessory anterolateral incision may be necessary for PLC reconstruction.

Multiple fixation strategies exist, including bony tunnels with interference screws, staples, and
suture anchor fixation. Avulsions may be managed via screw fixation if fragments at amenable.

Surgical Fracture Fixation
The author of this lesson prefers to use posterior tibial tendon allograft for acute
ACL/PCL reconstruction. Meniscal tears/avulsions also should be addressed. Substance
tears can be repaired with the use of nonabsorbable suture. Root avulsions can be
repaired with the use of suture anchors or bone tunnels. Rim avulsions can be
reattached with the use of suture anchors or nonabsorbable suture if peripheral soft
tissue is present.
Postoperative Management
Hinged knee brace locked in slight flexion for 2 weeks postoperatively until wounds are healed
Motion initiated at 2 weeks postoperatively
Touch-down weight bearing for 6 weeks postoperatively
Discontinue brace and transition to weight bearing as tolerated at 6 weeks postoperatively

Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Acute repair/reconstruction has historically been associated with a higher incidence
(20%) of arthrofibrosis requiring surgical management. In a more recent series, early
motion decreased surgical release to less than 5%.4 Heterotopic bone has been a
problem, especially in polytrauma patients, and prophylaxis may be considered.

Early repair and reconstruction (<3 weeks postinjury) of all damaged ligaments was associated

Arthroscopic Reconstruction
Late reconstruction of all ligaments has been routine for most surgeons. In a
randomized controlled trial, late reconstruction was associated with a lower incidence of
ligament failure if a hinged external fixator was applied. Staged management with early
repair of the collateral ligaments and delayed arthroscopic cruciate ligament
reconstruction is associated with a high incidence (30%) of late loosening5 (Resource 2).

Surgical Approaches
Arthroscopic reconstruction can be performed more 3 weeks postinjury. Standard anterior
portals and any necessary accessory portals are used. An open lateral incision is necessary if
posterolateral reconstruction is planned.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
Fractures are approached in standard fashion as necessary, with open or arthroscopic
management of ligaments.

range of motion and touch-down weightbearing for 6 weeks

Complications
Instability
Persistent laxity and inadequate restoration of soft tissue tensioning may lead to instability.
Residual instability (often related to failure to recognize and manage all components of the
initial injury).
Patients treated nonsurgically have a high incidence of instability.
Stiffness
Arthrofibrosis may be higher with open versus arthroscopic management; however, new
changes in protocol may limit the discrepancy.

Stiffness
Arthrofibrosis may be caused by heterotopic ossification (incidence of 26% to 43%) and
scarring about the capsule (Figure 21). Terminal extension and 10° to 15° of terminal
flexion are commonly lost (Figure 22). If the stiffness is severely limiting, manipulation
under anesthesia or arthroscopic or open lysis of the adhesions may be indicated. If
stiffness is caused by heterotopic bone, resection may be performed.

Postoperative Rehabilitation

Postoperative Rehabilitation
Traditionally patients were instructed to remain non–weight bearing for 6 weeks with the
knee braced in full extension; however, a recent trend advocates earlier motion and less
weight-bearing restrictions. Progressive range of motion and closed kinetic chain
exercises are initiated at approximately 4 to 6 weeks. Return to unrestricted activity
(sports, heavy labor) may take as long as 9 months or more.
Outcomes
Based on available data, repair and reconstruction of acute knee dislocations may lead to good
outcomes; however, patients likely will have some residual deficit, especially in patients who
sustain high-energy injuries and patients who undergo four-ligament reconstruction6
(Resource 3).
In a study of 85 patients treated via a combination of open and arthroscopic surgical
management of knee dislocations within 3 weeks postinjury, Engebretsen et al3 reported a
median Lysholm Knee Scale score of 83 and a median Tegner activity score of 5. Patients could
perform activity on a regular basis and scored above 83% on the single-leg hop test compared
with the uninjured side. Patients who sustained high-energy trauma and patients who
sustained an injury involving all four ligaments had poorer outcomes. In another study of 47
patients who underwent early open surgical treatment (acute repair or reconstruction of all
damaged structures) for the management of multiligamentous injuries (type KD III through
type KD V), 32% reported Tegner activity scores between 7 and 10. The mean Lysholm Knee
Scale score among these patients was 75.4. No patients reported loosening requiring revision
at 12 months postoperatively, and 4 of the 47 patients underwent manipulation or lysis of
adhesions.4
